title: Bridges: More Than a Way Across
description: At our last meeting, club members voted to focus on bridges! One bridge my family sometimes drives over has been reduced to alternating one-lane traffic. Another is part of our walks with our dog at Wilson Mill. They made me realize that bridges are about much more than getting from one side to the other.

sections.heading: A bridge we still need to cross
A bridge we visit just to enjoy
What can our club learn from them?

details.heading: Why bridges?
details.body:
At our last club meeting, we voted on what we wanted to explore first. The students who were there chose bridges!

I think it's a great place to start. We cross bridges when we're driving somewhere, walking on a trail, or just going about our day. Most of the time, we don't think much about them. I certainly didn't always stop to wonder what was holding the road up, or why a bridge was built in that particular spot.

But recently, two bridges near Bedford made me look at them differently. One is a bridge my family occasionally drives across, and right now it's hard not to worry about it. The other is somewhere we go for walks with our dog, and it has some of my favorite little memories. Both have stories worth exploring.

details.heading: A bridge we still need to cross
details.body:
Sometimes we drive over the Hart–Desiato Memorial Bridge on Route 225, between Bedford and Carlisle. Lately, getting across means waiting at a temporary traffic light while cars from the other direction take their turn. Only one lane is in use at a time.

I know that the traffic lights are there for a reason, but it's still concerning to think that a bridge we depend on needs such serious attention. What happened underneath it? And how do engineers decide when a bridge needs repairs, restrictions, or a completely new design?

I looked into it. According to Bedford's MassDOT bridge update, timber support piles on the southern portion of the bridge have deteriorated. Repairs to the deck have been completed, but the one-lane traffic pattern keeps vehicles away from the affected area while work on the supports is being planned. MassDOT is also considering a full replacement, according to The Bedford Citizen's August 2026 report. The restriction is a safety precaution, not proof that the bridge is unsafe to use as directed. The Bedford Citizen's report also includes photographs of the deteriorated timber piling—something that makes the problem much easier to picture.

There's something else important about this bridge: its name. It honors John Hart and Travis Desiato, two former Bedford High School students who served in the military. The bridge was officially named in their honor in 2017, and the community gathered for a dedication in 2018. It's not just a piece of infrastructure. It's also a memorial and part of Bedford's history.

So how do we keep a bridge safe and useful for the people crossing it now, while respecting what it means to the people who remember its history? That's an engineering question, but also a community question.

details.heading: A bridge we visit just to enjoy
details.body:
Then there's the bridge at Wilson Mill. My family and I go hiking around Wilson Mill Park with our dog all the time. The trails, the pond, and the view of the water make it such a nice place to spend an afternoon. It's the kind of place where we end up stopping to look around instead of just trying to get somewhere.

I remember one day when we saw so many tadpoles in the water, and little frogs too! It's such a small thing, but it's one of the memories I associate with that place.

Wilson Mill has its own history. A corn mill was built by Vine Brook in 1685, and later mills used the site too. You can still see traces of that history near the bridge, according to a local history of Wilson Mill. Bedford's trail map also shows how the paths wind around Mill Pond and the brook.

I love that a bridge can be more than a shortcut. It can help us experience nature and connect us to the history of a place. That's another side of civil engineering that we don't always notice.

details.heading: What can our club learn from them?
details.body:
These two bridges are very different. One carries traffic between towns and needs ongoing engineering attention. The other is part of a place where people walk, explore, and enjoy the water. But both make me ask the same question: how can we design things that work well for the communities around them?

As we begin our bridge project, I want us to look at how bridges carry weight, how different designs use materials, and how engineers deal with wear over time. We can research real bridges around Bedford and Boston, and build and test our own models to see what works.

We're students, not bridge inspectors, so we won't be making our own claims about whether a real bridge is safe. But we can learn how engineers make those decisions—and maybe start noticing the bridges around us a little differently.

If you have a bridge you think our club should look at, bring it up at our next meeting! I'd love to hear which ones matter to you, and why.

details.heading: Did you know?
details.body:
A bridge with a history: The Hart–Desiato Bridge was named in 2017 in honor of Private First Class John Hart and Marine Lance Corporal Travis Desiato. Both graduated from Bedford High School, and the memorial was dedicated in 2018. Sources: Massachusetts General Court and The Bedford Citizen.

Why the one-lane traffic? As of the August 19, 2026 update, deck repairs were finished, but deteriorated timber support piles still needed repairs. The alternating one-lane traffic pattern keeps vehicles away from the affected portion. Source: The Bedford Citizen, August 2026.

A bridge near centuries of history: A corn mill was recorded at the Wilson Mill site on Vine Brook in 1685. Today the area includes trails around Mill Pond. Sources: Wilson Mill history and Bedford trail map.
